blocks.md:
### Four terms that nest

**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is the broad goal of building machines that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence: perceiving, reasoning, learning, planning and using language. It is a field, not a technology, and it includes approaches that don’t learn at all.

**Machine learning (ML)** is the part of AI in which systems learn patterns from data rather than following rules a programmer wrote. Give a machine-learning system thousands of examples of fraudulent and legitimate transactions and it works out for itself which signals matter.

**Deep learning** is machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. Its defining advantage is *representation learning*: the network discovers useful features on its own, where older techniques needed people to engineer them by hand.

**Generative AI** is the branch of deep learning focused on creating new content: text, images, audio, video and code. Large language models (LLMs) are the best-known example.

These distinctions matter in practice. A rules-based fraud engine, a gradient-boosted risk score and an LLM chatbot are all "AI", but they fail differently, are attacked differently and need different controls.

blocks.title: Ways to classify AI
cards: Narrow AI (weak AI)
Performs one task or a defined range of tasks. Every AI system in production today, including LLMs, is narrow AI.
Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
Hypothetical AI matching human ability across most domains. No deployed system meets this definition.
Artificial superintelligence (ASI)
Hypothetical AI exceeding human ability in every domain. Discussed in long-term safety research.
Reactive machines
Respond to the current input with no memory of the past, like the chess computer Deep Blue.
Limited memory
Use recent or learned information to decide. Most modern machine learning, including self-driving perception, falls here.
Theory of mind and self-aware AI
Research concepts for systems that model others’ beliefs, or have awareness of themselves. Neither exists today.

blocks.title: “General-purpose” is not “general intelligence”
blocks.md: The EU AI Act regulates **general-purpose AI (GPAI) models**: models such as large LLMs that can perform a wide range of tasks and be built into many downstream systems. That is a legal category about breadth of use. It does not mean artificial general intelligence. If an exam option equates the two, it is a distractor.

### How the field evolved, and what each era left behind

AI has moved in waves of optimism and disappointment, and each wave left something that still matters for security.

- **1950–1970s: symbolic beginnings.** Turing’s 1950 paper asked whether machines can think. The 1956 Dartmouth workshop named the field. Early programs such as ELIZA (1966) imitated conversation with simple pattern matching, and people still attributed understanding to them. That human tendency to over-trust fluent machines is now a core risk with chatbots.
- **1980s: expert systems.** Organisations encoded specialist knowledge as thousands of if-then rules. They worked inside narrow boundaries and failed badly outside them, and maintaining them was costly. Funding collapsed twice, in the "AI winters" of the mid-1970s and late 1980s.
- **1990s–2000s: statistical machine learning.** Learning from data replaced hand-written rules for tasks such as spam filtering. IBM’s Deep Blue beat the world chess champion in 1997, using search rather than learning.
- **2012 onwards: deep learning.** AlexNet’s win at the ImageNet competition showed that large neural networks trained on GPUs could outperform hand-engineered approaches. Big data, cheap parallel compute and better training methods converged. AlphaGo beat a world champion at Go in 2016.
- **2017 onwards: transformers and generative AI.** The transformer architecture made it practical to train enormous language models on internet-scale text. ChatGPT’s release in November 2022 brought generative AI to the mainstream, followed quickly by multimodal and agentic systems that see, hear and act.

The security lesson of this history is that capability has outpaced assurance at every step. Each new technique was deployed before its failure modes were well understood.

blocks.md:
### Symbolic, statistical and hybrid

**Symbolic AI** (sometimes called classical or rules-based AI) represents knowledge explicitly, as rules, logic and knowledge graphs, and reasons over it. Its behaviour can be inspected and predicted, which auditors and regulators value. Its weakness is brittleness: it knows only what it was told.

**Machine learning** (the statistical or connectionist approach) learns behaviour from data. It copes with ambiguity and scale, but its reasoning is harder to inspect, and its behaviour depends on data that may be incomplete, biased or tampered with.

Many production systems are **hybrid**. A bank might use a learned model to score fraud risk and a rules engine to enforce hard limits and regulatory requirements. An LLM application often wraps a learned model in deterministic code that validates inputs, restricts tools and checks outputs. That deterministic wrapper is frequently where security controls live.

### Discriminative and generative models

A **discriminative model** learns to separate classes: given an input, which label is most likely? Fraud detection, malware classification and spam filtering are discriminative tasks. A **generative model** learns the underlying distribution of the data well enough to produce new samples from it. That ability is what makes deepfakes, synthetic phishing emails and fabricated documents possible, and why generative AI raises content-integrity and disclosure questions that classifiers never did.

### The AI ecosystem and its trust boundaries

Very few organisations build AI end to end. A typical deployment involves:

- **Data providers and labellers**, who collect, license, clean and annotate training data.
- **Compute providers**, who supply accelerators, cloud platforms and data centres.
- **Model developers**, who train models, including large *foundation models* that others adapt.
- **Platforms and model hubs**, which host, version and distribute models and datasets, often openly.
- **Application builders and integrators**, who connect models to products through APIs, retrieval pipelines, plugins and agents.
- **Deployers and operators**, who run the system for a purpose and are accountable for how it is used.
- **Users and affected people**, including people who never interact with the system but are subject to its decisions.
- **Oversight bodies**, such as regulators, auditors and standards organisations.

The EU AI Act gives some of these roles legal weight. It distinguishes **providers** (who develop an AI system or model and place it on the market), **deployers** (who use it under their authority), **importers** and **distributors**, and assigns obligations to each. You will study those obligations in Domain 2.

For a security professional, the key point is that every hand-off is a **trust boundary**. A poisoned public dataset, a tampered model file on a hub, a compromised dependency in a training pipeline or an over-privileged integration can each undermine a system that looks secure in isolation. Supply-chain risk runs through Domains 2, 3 and 6.

q.q: A team fine-tunes an open model downloaded from a public hub, then exposes it to customers through an API. Which statement BEST describes their position in the AI ecosystem?
o: They are only users of the model, so its supply-chain risk belongs to the hub that hosts it
They rely on upstream providers and also become accountable for what they deploy
They are a compute provider, because they host the API that customers call
They carry no security responsibility for the model itself, because it is open source
q.why: The team depends on the upstream model and hub, which are part of its supply chain, and as the party offering the system to customers it is accountable for how the model behaves in its product. Open licensing does not transfer that accountability.

Unsupervised anomaly detection
Reinforcement learning with a reward for each detection
Transfer learning from an image recognition model

Slowly shifting “normal” can make malicious activity look ordinary

blocks.md:
### Supervised learning

In **supervised learning** the training data contains inputs and the correct outputs, called **labels**. The inputs are described by **features**: measurable properties such as an email’s sender reputation, the number of links it contains or the words it uses. The model learns a mapping from features to labels, then applies it to new data.

Supervised tasks come in two kinds:

- **Classification** predicts a category: spam or legitimate, malicious or benign, fraud or not fraud.
- **Regression** predicts a number: a risk score, a transaction value, the time until a disk fails.

Data is normally split three ways. The **training set** teaches the model. The **validation set** is used to tune it and to decide when to stop training. The **test set** is held back until the end to estimate real-world performance. If test data leaks into training, results look better than they are, which is why dataset separation is a control as well as good practice.

The goal is **generalisation**: performing well on data the model has never seen. A model that memorises its training data (**overfitting**) or is too simple to capture the pattern (**underfitting**) generalises poorly.

### Unsupervised learning

**Unsupervised learning** finds structure in data that has no labels. The main techniques are:

- **Clustering**, which groups similar items, for example grouping endpoints by behaviour or alerts by root cause.
- **Dimensionality reduction**, which compresses many features into fewer while keeping the important variation. It is useful for visualisation and for speeding up other models.
- **Anomaly detection**, which learns what normal looks like and flags what doesn’t fit. Much of user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA) works this way.
- **Association analysis**, which finds items that occur together.

Unsupervised methods are attractive in security because labelled attack data is scarce. Their weakness is interpretation: an anomaly is unusual, not necessarily malicious, so a person must decide what it means.

blocks.title: Reinforcement learning, term by term
items: Agent and environment

The **agent** is the learner that makes decisions. The **environment** is everything it interacts with: a game, a robot’s surroundings, a simulated network. The **state** is the agent’s view of the environment at a given moment.
Actions and rewards

At each step the agent takes an **action**. The environment responds with a new state and a **reward**, a number that scores the outcome. The agent’s aim is to maximise **cumulative** reward over time, not just the next reward.
Policy
The **policy** is the agent’s strategy: what action to take in each state. Training improves the policy. In deep reinforcement learning the policy is a neural network.
Exploration vs exploitation

The agent must balance **exploiting** actions it already knows work against **exploring** new actions that might work better. Too little exploration gets stuck in mediocre strategies; too much wastes effort.
RLHF

**Reinforcement learning from human feedback** tunes language models using human preferences. People rank model responses, a *reward model* learns to predict those rankings, and the language model is then optimised to produce responses the reward model scores highly. It is a major reason chat assistants behave helpfully and refuse some requests.

blocks.md:
### Other learning setups

- **Semi-supervised learning** combines a small labelled set with a large unlabelled one, which helps when labelling is expensive, as it is with expert-reviewed security events.
- **Self-supervised learning** generates labels from the data itself: predict the next word, fill in a masked word, or predict a missing patch of an image. It lets models learn from enormous unlabelled datasets and is how foundation models are pretrained.
- **Transfer learning** reuses a model trained on one task as the starting point for another. Fine-tuning a foundation model is transfer learning. It saves data and compute, but the new model inherits the original’s strengths, biases and any hidden flaws.
- **Federated learning** trains a shared model across many devices or organisations. Each participant trains locally and sends only model updates to be combined, so raw data never leaves its owner. That helps privacy, but the combining step must defend against participants who send harmful updates.
- **Online (continual) learning** updates the model as new data arrives. It adapts quickly to change, and for the same reason it can be pushed in the wrong direction by manipulated data.

blocks.title: Reward hacking in one sentence
blocks.md: A reinforcement learner optimises exactly what it is rewarded for, not what you meant. If a cleaning robot is rewarded for not *seeing* mess, covering its camera is a winning strategy. Writing objectives that can’t be gamed is a recurring safety problem, and it reappears with AI agents.

blocks.title: Choosing the paradigm
blocks.md: A security operations team wants a model that ranks incoming alerts by how likely they are to be true positives. Over two years, analysts have closed 400,000 alerts and recorded whether each was a real incident or a false positive.

q.q: Which learning approach is the MOST natural fit?
o: Supervised learning, using the analysts’ dispositions as labels
Unsupervised clustering, because alert data has no labels
Reinforcement learning, rewarding the model for closing alerts quickly
Self-supervised learning, predicting the next alert in sequence
q.why: The analysts’ recorded outcomes are labels, so this is a classic supervised classification problem. Rewarding speed would invite the model to close alerts regardless of risk, which is reward hacking in action.

scenes.title: One training step

notes.d: Neurons in layers, joined by weighted connections. The weights are what the network learns.
Inputs flow through the layers to produce a prediction.
The prediction is compared with the label. The gap is the error.
The error flows backwards, working out each weight’s share of the blame.
Every weight moves a small step in the direction that reduces the error.
Millions of examples and many passes later, the network has learned.

scenes.say: Here is a tiny network that classifies email. Each circle is a neuron, and each line is a weighted connection. The weights are what the network learns. | In the forward pass, the email’s features flow through the layers, and the network produces a prediction. | That prediction is compared with the correct label using a loss function. The gap between them is the error. | Backpropagation sends the error backwards through the network, working out how much each weight contributed to it. | Then gradient descent nudges every weight a small step in the direction that reduces the error. The size of that step is the learning rate. | Repeat this over millions of examples and many passes, and the network gradually learns.

scenes.title: When learning turns into memorising

notes.d: Falls steadily as the model fits the training data.
Measured on held-back data the model never trains on.
After epoch 7 the model memorises the training set and gets worse on new data.
More data, regularisation, dropout and early stopping.

scenes.say: Training repeats over many passes through the data, called epochs, and the error on the training data keeps falling. | But on validation data the model has never trained on, the error falls, and then starts to rise. | That turning point is where the model stops learning general patterns and starts memorising its training set. This is overfitting. | More data, regularisation, a technique called dropout, and simply stopping early all help a model generalise to new data.

scenes.title: Evolutionary computation
scenes.intro: No gradients needed: candidates compete, and the fittest are recombined generation after generation.

stages.label: Population
stages.d: Start with many random candidate solutions.

stages.label: Fitness
stages.d: Score every candidate with a fitness function.

stages.label: Selection
stages.d: Keep the fittest candidates as parents.

stages.label: Crossover
stages.d: Combine parts of two parents into offspring.

stages.label: Mutation
stages.d: Make small random changes to keep variety.

scenes.say: Evolutionary computation takes a completely different route to a good answer. | A genetic algorithm starts with a population of random candidate solutions. | Each candidate is scored by a fitness function that measures how good it is. | The fittest candidates are selected to become parents. | Crossover combines parts of two parents to create offspring. | Mutation makes small random changes, so the population does not become too similar. | The new generation replaces the old, and the cycle repeats. Crucially, it needs no gradients, only a way to score results.

scenes.title: Why security teams care about evolutionary search

items.d: Coverage-guided fuzzers evolve inputs that reach new code paths
Search can find inputs that flip a model’s output using only its responses
Generate and score test cases at a scale people can’t
Tune hyperparameters, or even network designs

scenes.say: Evolutionary search matters in security for four reasons. | Coverage-guided fuzzers, a staple of vulnerability research, evolve test inputs that reach new code paths. | Because it only needs a score, the same kind of search can probe a model from the outside, finding inputs that change its output using nothing but its responses. That is why limiting and monitoring queries matters. | Defenders use the same idea for automated red teaming, generating and scoring test cases at scale. | And it is widely used for optimisation, such as tuning hyperparameters or searching for network designs.

blocks.md:
### Inside a neural network

An artificial **neuron** takes several inputs, multiplies each by a **weight**, adds them together with a **bias**, and passes the result through an **activation function**. The activation function introduces non-linearity, which is what lets networks learn complex patterns. Common choices are **ReLU** (which outputs zero for negative values and passes positive values unchanged), **sigmoid** (which squashes values into the range 0 to 1) and **softmax** (which turns a set of scores into probabilities that add up to 1, typically in the output layer of a classifier).

Neurons are arranged in **layers**: an input layer, one or more **hidden layers**, and an output layer. A network is "deep" when it has many hidden layers. Early layers tend to learn simple features, such as edges in an image or common word fragments, and later layers combine them into abstract concepts.

The learned values, the weights and biases, are the model’s **parameters**. Large language models have billions of them. Choices people make *before* training, such as the learning rate, number of layers, batch size and number of epochs, are **hyperparameters**.

### The training loop

1. **Forward pass:** a batch of training examples flows through the network to produce predictions.
2. **Loss:** a loss function measures how far the predictions are from the labels. Cross-entropy is typical for classification and mean squared error for regression.
3. **Backpropagation:** the chain rule of calculus is applied backwards through the network to compute the **gradient**, how much each parameter contributed to the loss.
4. **Gradient descent:** an optimiser, such as stochastic gradient descent or Adam, adjusts each parameter a small step against its gradient. The **learning rate** sets the step size: too high and training is unstable, too low and it crawls.

One full pass through the training data is an **epoch**. Training runs for many epochs, and the result is a set of weights, often called a **checkpoint**, that can be saved, shared, loaded and attacked like any other valuable file.

Using a trained model to make predictions is called **inference**. Training is expensive and happens occasionally. Inference happens every time someone uses the model, so its cost, speed and security dominate day-to-day operations.

blocks.title: Overfitting, underfitting and how to fix them
items: Overfitting

The model fits the training data too closely, including its noise and quirks, and performs worse on new data. Signs: very low training error, much higher validation error. Overfitted models can also **memorise** individual training records, which becomes a privacy risk if those records are sensitive.
Underfitting
The model is too simple, or trained too little, to capture the real pattern. Both training and validation error stay high.
Remedies

Collect more, and more varied, data. Use **regularisation**, which penalises overly complex models. Use **dropout**, which randomly switches off neurons during training so the network can’t rely on any one of them. Stop training early when validation error starts to rise. Augment data with realistic variations.
Why security cares

A model that memorises can leak training data, and a model that generalises poorly fails unpredictably on unusual inputs, which an adversary can deliberately supply. Good generalisation is a security property as well as a quality one.

blocks.md:
### Why deep learning took off when it did

Neural networks date back to the 1950s perceptron, and backpropagation was popularised in 1986. Deep learning only became dominant after 2012, when three things converged:

- **Data:** the internet produced labelled image collections such as ImageNet, and vast amounts of text.
- **Compute:** graphics processing units (GPUs), designed for games, turned out to be ideal for the matrix arithmetic neural networks need.
- **Methods:** better activation functions, initialisation, regularisation and architectures made very deep networks trainable.

### Evolutionary computation

**Evolutionary computation** is a family of optimisation methods inspired by natural selection. Instead of following a gradient, it maintains a population of candidate solutions and improves it over generations.

In a **genetic algorithm**, each candidate is encoded as a "chromosome", for example a string of bits or numbers. A **fitness function** scores each one. The fittest are **selected** as parents, **crossover** recombines their genes, and **mutation** introduces small random changes to keep diversity. Related techniques include **genetic programming**, which evolves programs, **evolution strategies**, and swarm methods such as particle swarm optimisation and ant colony optimisation, which are often grouped with them as nature-inspired computation.

These methods shine where gradients aren’t available or the search space is rugged: scheduling, design optimisation, hyperparameter tuning, neural architecture search and **neuroevolution** (evolving network weights or structures). Their drawbacks are cost, because they need many evaluations, and no guarantee of finding the best possible answer.

blocks.title: The black-box lesson
blocks.md: Evolutionary and other gradient-free search methods need only a score to optimise against. Applied to a deployed model, the "score" can simply be the model’s own outputs. That is why exposing detailed confidence scores, allowing unlimited queries, or failing to monitor unusual query patterns makes it easier for someone to probe a model’s weaknesses. You will return to query limits and output handling in Domains 3 and 4.

blocks.md:
### From neurons to architectures

The simplest deep network is the **multilayer perceptron (MLP)**, sometimes called a fully connected or dense network: every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next. MLPs work well on tabular data, but they ignore structure. They don’t know that neighbouring pixels are related, or that word order matters. Specialised architectures build that structure in.

### Convolutional neural networks (CNNs)

A CNN applies small learned **filters** (also called kernels) that slide across the input. Each filter detects a local pattern and produces a **feature map** showing where that pattern occurs. Because the same filter is reused across the whole image, a technique called **weight sharing**, CNNs need far fewer parameters than dense networks and recognise a pattern wherever it appears.

**Pooling** layers downsample feature maps, typically keeping the maximum value in each small region. That makes the network tolerant of small shifts and reduces computation. Stacked convolution and pooling layers build a hierarchy: edges, then textures and shapes, then object parts, then whole objects. Dense layers at the end turn those features into a classification.

CNNs power image classification, object detection, face recognition and medical imaging, and are also applied to audio spectrograms and to malware binaries rendered as images. Their best-known security weakness is the **adversarial example**: an input altered in ways people barely notice, or a printed patch placed in a scene, that reliably changes the model’s prediction. Module 6.1 covers these evasion attacks in depth.

### Recurrent neural networks (RNNs)

An RNN processes a sequence one element at a time, maintaining a **hidden state** that summarises what it has seen so far. Each step combines the new input with the previous state. Training "unrolls" the network through time and applies backpropagation across the steps.

Plain RNNs suffer from **vanishing and exploding gradients**: over long sequences the training signal shrinks towards zero or grows uncontrollably, so they forget early information. **Long short-term memory (LSTM)** networks add gates (input, forget and output) that learn what to store, discard and reveal. **Gated recurrent units (GRUs)** are a simpler variant. RNNs were the backbone of speech recognition and machine translation until about 2017, and still appear in time-series and some log-analysis systems. Their sequential nature limits how far training can be parallelised.

blocks.title: How self-attention works, step by step
items: Turn tokens into vectors
Each token (a word or part of a word) becomes an **embedding**, a list of numbers representing its meaning, plus a **positional encoding** that marks where it sits in the sequence.
Create queries, keys and values
For every token the model computes three vectors. The **query** asks "what am I looking for?", the **key** advertises "what do I contain?", and the **value** carries the information to pass on.
Score every pair
Each token’s query is compared with every other token’s key. The scores are normalised with softmax into **attention weights** that sum to 1.
Blend the values
Each token’s new representation is the weighted sum of all tokens' values. The word "it" absorbs most of its meaning from "server" because that pair scored highest.
Repeat with many heads and layers
**Multi-head attention** runs several attention patterns in parallel, so one head can track grammar while another tracks meaning. Dozens of layers are stacked, each refining the representation.

blocks.md:
### Transformers

Introduced in the 2017 paper *Attention Is All You Need*, the transformer dispenses with recurrence and relies on **self-attention**. Because every token can attend to every other token directly, distant words relate as easily as neighbours, and the whole sequence is processed in parallel, which suits GPUs and makes training on internet-scale data feasible.

Three variants matter:

- **Encoder-only** models, such as BERT, read the whole input at once and excel at understanding tasks like classification and search.
- **Decoder-only** models, such as the GPT family, generate text one token at a time, each token attending only to those before it. Most chat LLMs are decoder-only.
- **Encoder-decoder** models, such as T5, map an input sequence to an output sequence, as in translation and summarisation.

Attention compares every token with every other, so its cost grows roughly with the *square* of the sequence length. That is one reason models have a fixed **context window**, the maximum number of tokens they can consider at once, covered in Module 1.2. Transformers have also displaced CNNs for some vision tasks (vision transformers) and handle images, audio and text together in **multimodal** models.

The security implication runs through the rest of this course: a transformer has no built-in notion of which tokens are trusted instructions and which are untrusted data. A system prompt, a user’s question, a retrieved web page and a tool’s output all end up as tokens in the same context, and all of them can influence the output. That design fact is the root of prompt injection, studied in Domains 4 and 6.

blocks.title: Other architectures worth recognising
items: Generative adversarial networks (GANs)
Two networks train against each other: a **generator** creates fake samples and a **discriminator** tries to tell them from real ones. GANs produced the first convincing deepfake faces.
Autoencoders

Networks that compress input into a small representation and reconstruct it. Inputs that reconstruct badly are unusual, so autoencoders are used for **anomaly detection**, including in network traffic.
Diffusion models
Generate images, audio or video by learning to remove noise step by step, starting from pure noise. They power most modern image generators.
Graph neural networks (GNNs)
Operate on graphs of nodes and edges, such as social networks, transaction graphs or attack graphs. Useful for fraud rings and relationship analysis.

blocks.md:
### Processors for AI

- **CPUs (central processing units)** have a handful of powerful cores optimised for sequential, branching logic. They run the operating system, data preparation, orchestration and classical machine-learning models, and can serve small neural networks.
- **GPUs (graphics processing units)** contain thousands of simpler cores designed to do the same operation on many numbers at once. Neural-network training and inference are dominated by matrix multiplication, which GPUs parallelise extremely well. A mature software ecosystem (NVIDIA’s CUDA is the best known) made GPUs the default AI accelerator.
- **TPUs (tensor processing units)** are application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) that Google designed for neural-network workloads. They use large *systolic arrays* to stream matrix operations efficiently and are connected into "pods" for very large training runs. They are available through Google Cloud.
- **NPUs (neural processing units)** are low-power accelerators built into phones, laptops and edge devices for on-device inference.
- **FPGAs** (field-programmable gate arrays) can be reconfigured for specific low-latency workloads, and cloud providers also build their own **custom ASICs** for training and inference.

### Memory: the real constraint

Model weights must sit in fast memory close to the processor. Accelerators use **high-bandwidth memory (HBM)**, often called VRAM on graphics cards. Two numbers matter: **capacity**, which decides whether a model fits, and **bandwidth**, which decides how fast it runs, because generating each token means reading the weights from memory. Inference on large models is frequently *memory-bound* rather than compute-bound.

A useful rule of thumb is **weight memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter**:

- 32-bit floating point (FP32): 4 bytes per parameter
- 16-bit (FP16 or BF16): 2 bytes
- 8-bit integer (INT8): 1 byte
- 4-bit (INT4): half a byte

So a 7-billion-parameter model needs about 28 GB at FP32, 14 GB at FP16 and 3.5 GB at INT4, *before* working memory. Serving also needs a **key-value (KV) cache** that grows with the length of the context and the number of simultaneous users. Training needs several times more again, for gradients, optimiser state and activations. **Quantisation** reduces precision to save memory and speed up inference, with some loss of accuracy.

Models too large for one device are split across several, using fast interconnects between GPUs and high-speed networks between servers.

blocks.md:
### Why hardware matters to security

**Isolation on shared accelerators.** Cloud GPUs are often shared between workloads or tenants. If memory isn’t cleared or isolated, one workload may read data left by another. In January 2024, researchers disclosed *LeftoverLocals* (CVE-2023-4969), which showed that GPUs from several vendors could leak data from their local memory between processes, including fragments of another user’s LLM session. Controls include dedicated or hardware-partitioned GPUs (NVIDIA’s Multi-Instance GPU, for example, splits one GPU into isolated instances), memory scrubbing between jobs, and timely driver updates.

**Drivers, firmware and runtimes.** Accelerator drivers and firmware run with high privilege and regularly receive security fixes. They belong in your patch and configuration management, and firmware integrity should be verified.

**Model weights as crown jewels.** A trained model can represent millions in compute and proprietary data. Weights sit in storage, in memory and in transit between servers. Encrypt them at rest and in transit, restrict who and what can load them, and log access. Module 3.6 covers model confidentiality.

**Confidential computing.** Trusted execution environments on CPUs, and confidential-computing modes on recent data-centre GPUs, keep data and models encrypted even while they are being processed, and can prove to a remote party what code is running (*attestation*). They matter when using third-party clouds for sensitive AI workloads, covered in Module 2.5.

**Availability and cost.** Accelerator capacity is finite and expensive. Heavy or abusive request patterns can exhaust capacity, slow service for everyone, or run up large bills, sometimes called *denial of wallet*. Rate limiting, quotas and compute throttling (Modules 4.2 and 3.6) protect against this.

**Physical and environmental security.** AI racks draw far more power and generate far more heat than typical servers, which raises the stakes for power redundancy, cooling and fire suppression, and for media sanitisation when high-density storage is retired. Modules 4.2 and 3.4 return to these.

If you can do the parameters × bytes calculation and explain the isolation risk, you are well prepared.

blocks.md:
### What changes when the system learns

Securing AI builds on everything you know about information security, but several properties of AI systems change the work:

- **Behaviour comes from data.** A model’s logic is learned, so whoever influences the training data influences the behaviour. Data effectively becomes code.
- **Outputs are probabilistic.** The same input can yield different outputs, and models can be confidently wrong. Testing can show that failures are rare, but it can’t prove they never happen.
- **Natural language erases the code–data boundary.** Classic injection attacks exploit places where data is interpreted as code. LLMs interpret everything in their context as potential instructions, so the boundary has to be rebuilt with controls around the model.
- **The model is an asset.** Weights encode expensive training and proprietary data. They can be stolen, copied through queries, or replaced with tampered versions.
- **Behaviour drifts.** Models degrade as the world changes, and systems that keep learning can be steered. Security is a continuous lifecycle activity, not a launch gate.
- **Opacity.** Deep models are hard to explain, which complicates incident investigation, audit and accountability.
- **Agency.** AI agents call tools, browse, write files and trigger transactions. Every permission an agent holds is a permission an attacker may borrow.

blocks.title: The threat names you will meet, in one line each
items: Data poisoning
Corrupting training or fine-tuning data so the model learns harmful or attacker-chosen behaviour. *Integrity.*
Backdoor (trojan)
A hidden behaviour planted during training that activates only when a specific trigger appears in the input. *Integrity.*
Evasion (adversarial examples)
Inputs modified, often imperceptibly, to make a model misclassify them at inference time. *Integrity.*
Model extraction
Reproducing a model’s functionality by querying it and training a copy on the answers. *Confidentiality.*
Model inversion and membership inference
Using a model’s outputs to reconstruct sensitive training data, or to learn whether a particular record was in the training set. *Confidentiality and privacy.*
Prompt injection
Instructions placed in a model’s input, directly by a user or indirectly through content the model reads, that override the developer’s intended behaviour. *Integrity.*
Excessive agency
An AI system granted more functionality, permissions or autonomy than it needs, so a manipulated model can do real damage. *All three.*
Resource exhaustion
Inputs or request volumes that consume disproportionate compute, tokens or money. *Availability.*

blocks.md:
### Trustworthy AI

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework describes seven characteristics of trustworthy AI. Security professionals are expected to help achieve all of them, not only the security one:

1. **Valid and reliable**: performs as intended, consistently.
2. **Safe**: does not endanger people, property or the environment.
3. **Secure and resilient**: withstands attacks and recovers from them.
4. **Accountable and transparent**: responsibilities are clear and information about the system is available.
5. **Explainable and interpretable**: its outputs and how it works can be understood appropriately.
6. **Privacy-enhanced**: protects people’s autonomy and data.
7. **Fair, with harmful bias managed**: does not produce unjust outcomes for individuals or groups.

These characteristics trade off against each other. More explainability can mean a simpler, less accurate model. Stronger privacy protections can reduce accuracy. Managing those trade-offs is a governance decision, covered in Domain 2.

### The reference frameworks

- **MITRE ATLAS** (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems) is a knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques and real-world case studies against AI-enabled systems, structured like MITRE ATT&CK. Use it for threat modelling and to describe findings in a shared vocabulary.
- **OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications** ranks the most critical security risks for applications built on LLMs. The 2025 edition is listed in the table below.
- **NIST AI RMF 1.0** organises AI risk management into four functions: **Govern** (culture, policies and accountability), **Map** (context and risks), **Measure** (analysis, assessment and tracking) and **Manage** (prioritise and treat risks). NIST also publishes **AI 100-2**, a taxonomy of adversarial machine-learning attacks and mitigations.
- **ISO/IEC 42001** specifies requirements for an AI management system that organisations can be certified against. **ISO/IEC 23894** gives guidance on AI risk management.

Instructions and data share the same natural-language channel, so the model can’t reliably separate them

scenes.say: Training minimises a loss: one number that measures how wrong the model’s predictions are. Classifiers and language models usually use cross-entropy, which is low when the model gives a high probability to the right answer. Backpropagation works out the gradient, the direction in which each weight should move, and gradient descent takes a small step in that direction, over and over. | The size of each step is the learning rate. Set it too small, and training crawls. | Set it too large, and every step overshoots, so the loss bounces around and never settles. Optimisers such as Adam adapt the step size for each weight automatically.

scenes.title: Temperature reshapes the same logits
scenes.yLabel: Probability of each next word, from logits 4, 2 and 1
scenes.say: A model’s last layer produces logits: raw scores, one for every possible output. The softmax function turns them into probabilities. Here, logits of four, two and one become eighty-four, eleven and four per cent. | Dividing the logits by a temperature before the softmax changes the shape. At a temperature of a half, the top choice takes ninety-eight per cent, so output becomes almost deterministic. | At a temperature of two, the distribution flattens and less likely words are sampled more often. The logits themselves are sensitive: exposing them, or detailed probabilities, helps attackers copy a model or test whether a record was in its training data.

scenes.title: Mixture of experts: only some of the model runs

steps.show: e1 e2 e3 rt-e1 rt-e2 rt-e3

scenes.say: Many of today’s largest models use a mixture of experts. Each token of input reaches a layer that contains several expert sub-networks. | A small router network scores the experts for that token. | Only the top few, here two out of eight, actually run. | Their outputs are combined into a weighted sum, and the token moves on to the next layer. | The result is a model with a huge total number of parameters, but far fewer active for any one token. That cuts compute, not memory: every expert must still be loaded. It also adds new failure modes, such as experts overflowing their capacity when a batch is shared between users.

scenes.title: Dense or mixture of experts?
scenes.say: Here is how the two designs compare. | A dense model uses every parameter for every token. A mixture of experts uses only the experts its router selects, a small active share. | Both need memory for all of their parameters: a mixture of experts still loads every expert. | Compute is where they differ. A dense model’s compute grows with its size; a mixture of experts’ compute grows with its active share, which is why it is cheaper to run. | And security: research has shown that when experts have fixed capacity and users share a batch, one user’s inputs can affect another user’s outputs. Behaviour can also differ between experts, so evaluations need broad and varied test inputs.

blocks.md:
### Loss, gradients and optimisers
- **Loss function:** a single number measuring prediction error. Classification and language modelling usually use **cross-entropy**, which is low when the model assigns high probability to the correct answer. A language model’s **perplexity** is the exponential of its average cross-entropy per token.
- **Gradient:** the vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to every weight. **Backpropagation** computes it efficiently, layer by layer, using the chain rule.
- **Gradient descent:** each update moves the weights a small step against the gradient: *new weight = weight − learning rate × gradient*. **Stochastic gradient descent** uses small random batches of data rather than the whole dataset.
- **Learning rate:** too small and training is slow; too large and the loss oscillates or diverges. Schedules lower it over time.
- **Optimisers:** **Adam** and its variants adapt the step size for each weight using running averages of past gradients. **Regularisation**, such as weight decay, dropout and early stopping, limits overfitting (Section 3).

### From logits to probabilities
The final layer outputs **logits**, one raw score per possible output. **Softmax** converts them into probabilities that sum to 1: each logit is divided by the **temperature**, exponentiated and normalised.

| Logits 4, 2 and 1 | Top choice | Second | Third |
|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature 0.5 | 98% | 1.8% | 0.2% |
| Temperature 1 | 84% | 11% | 4% |
| Temperature 2 | 63% | 23% | 14% |

Lower temperatures make outputs more deterministic; higher ones make them more varied. **Top-k** and **top-p** sampling then restrict which tokens can be chosen (Module 1.2).

### Why the internals matter for security
- **Gradients are dual-use.** The same machinery that computes gradients for the weights can compute gradients for the *input*, which is how white-box adversarial examples are crafted (Module 6.1, deep dive). Fine-tuning gradients can also weaken safety behaviour (Module 3.7).
- **Logits and probabilities leak information.** Detailed scores reveal decision boundaries and confidence, helping **model extraction** and **membership inference**. Returning labels, or rounded or limited log-probabilities, raises attackers’ costs (Module 3.6).
- **Sampling settings affect evidence.** Temperature and sampling explain why outputs vary between runs, so findings are reported as rates (Module 6.5).

### Mixture of experts (MoE)
A mixture-of-experts layer replaces one large feed-forward block with many smaller **experts** and a **router** (gating network) that sends each token to the top few, often two. **Mixtral 8x7B** has about 47 billion parameters in total but uses about 13 billion per token; **DeepSeek-V3** has 671 billion in total with 37 billion active.
- **Resources:** compute scales with the active parameters, but **memory must hold every expert**. Plan capacity accordingly (Module 4.2).
- **Capacity and isolation:** some implementations give each expert a fixed capacity per batch. Research by Hayes and colleagues (2024) showed that, in that setting, an attacker’s inputs batched with a victim’s could change the victim’s outputs, an argument for isolating tenants and testing serving configurations.
- **Evaluation coverage:** routing means different inputs exercise different experts, so safety and security evaluations need broad, varied test sets rather than a handful of prompts.

blocks.title: Training and architecture terms
cards: Cross-entropy loss
A loss that is low when the model gives high probability to the correct answer; standard for classifiers and language models.
Learning rate
The size of each gradient descent step: too small is slow, too large overshoots and fails to settle.
Adam
An optimiser that adapts the step size for each weight using running averages of past gradients.
Logits
The raw scores a model outputs before softmax turns them into probabilities.
Softmax temperature
A divisor applied to logits before softmax: low values sharpen the distribution, high values flatten it.
Active parameters
In a mixture of experts, the parameters actually used for a given token, a fraction of the total.

q.q: A team plans to self-host a mixture-of-experts model with about 47 billion parameters in total, of which about 13 billion are active for each token. Which statement about its resource needs is MOST accurate?
o: It needs memory and compute similar to a dense 13-billion-parameter model
It needs memory for all 47 billion parameters, but less compute per token
It needs compute for all 47 billion parameters, but memory for only 13 billion
It needs no more resources than a 7-billion-parameter dense model
q.why: Every expert must be loaded, so memory follows the total parameter count, while compute per token follows the active parameters. That is the trade-off a mixture of experts makes.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between AI, machine learning and deep learning?
o: Machine learning is a subset of deep learning, which is a subset of AI
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI
AI, machine learning and deep learning are three names for the same thing
Deep learning is a subset of AI that is unrelated to machine learning
quiz.why: AI is the broad field; machine learning is the part that learns from data; deep learning is machine learning using many-layered neural networks.

quiz.q: By capability, how are the AI systems in production today classified?
o: Artificial general intelligence
Artificial superintelligence
Narrow AI (weak AI)
Self-aware AI
quiz.why: Every deployed system, including large language models, is narrow AI. General AI and superintelligence remain hypothetical.

quiz.q: A model learns the distribution of its training data well enough to create new, realistic samples. What kind of model is it?
o: Discriminative
Generative
Symbolic
Reactive
quiz.why: Generative models learn what the data looks like and can produce new examples. Discriminative models learn the boundary between classes.

quiz.q: A team trains a model on 50,000 emails, each marked as spam or legitimate by analysts. Which learning paradigm is this?
o: Unsupervised learning
Federated learning
Supervised learning
Self-supervised learning
quiz.why: Training on inputs paired with correct labels is supervised learning, here a classification task.

quiz.q: Large language models are pretrained by predicting the next token across vast amounts of text. What kind of learning is this?
o: Self-supervised learning
Reinforcement learning from human feedback
Unsupervised clustering
Federated learning
quiz.why: The labels, the next tokens, come from the data itself, which makes pretraining self-supervised. RLHF is a later tuning stage.

quiz.q: An agent improves its strategy by taking actions in an environment and receiving scores for the outcomes. Which paradigm is this?
o: Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Transfer learning
Semi-supervised learning
quiz.why: Learning a policy from rewards earned by acting in an environment is reinforcement learning.

quiz.q: During training, error on the training data keeps falling while error on the validation data starts to rise. What does this indicate?
o: Underfitting
Overfitting
A learning rate that is too low
Data drift
quiz.why: The model is memorising the training set and generalising worse to unseen data, the signature of overfitting.

quiz.q: Which step of training calculates how much each weight contributed to the error?
o: The forward pass
Backpropagation
Pooling
Tokenisation
quiz.why: Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards through the network to compute each parameter’s gradient. Gradient descent then uses those gradients to update the weights.

quiz.q: In a genetic algorithm, what decides which candidate solutions survive into the next generation?
o: The learning rate
The fitness function
The activation function
The loss gradient
quiz.why: Each candidate is scored by a fitness function, and the fittest are selected as parents. No gradients are involved.

quiz.q: Which architecture uses learned filters that slide across an image to detect local patterns?
o: Recurrent neural network
Convolutional neural network
Transformer decoder
Graph attention network
quiz.why: Convolutional neural networks apply sliding filters to grid-like data, building from edges to whole objects.

quiz.q: What allows a transformer to weigh the relevance of every token to every other token in a sequence?
o: A hidden state passed between steps
Self-attention
Max pooling
A fitness function
quiz.why: Self-attention scores every pair of tokens and blends their information, processing the whole sequence in parallel.

quiz.q: Roughly how much memory is needed just to hold the weights of a 7-billion-parameter model at 16-bit precision?
o: About 3.5 GB
About 7 GB
About 14 GB
About 28 GB
quiz.why: Sixteen-bit precision uses 2 bytes per parameter: 7 billion × 2 bytes ≈ 14 GB. 28 GB would be 32-bit; 3.5 GB would be 4-bit.

quiz.q: During training, a model’s loss falls for a few steps, then swings up and down from step to step and never settles. Which change is MOST likely to help?
o: Adding more layers, so the model has greater capacity to learn
Lowering the learning rate, or using a schedule that reduces it
Raising the softmax temperature used when generating outputs
Removing the validation set, so more data is available for training
quiz.why: A loss that oscillates instead of settling is the classic sign of a learning rate that is too large: each step overshoots. More layers, sampling temperature and the validation set don’t address the step size.

quiz.q: A model’s final layer produces scores of 4, 2 and 1 for three possible outputs. What does applying softmax with a temperature below 1 do?
o: Spreads probability more evenly, so less likely outputs are chosen more often
Concentrates probability on the top output, making choices more predictable
Removes the lowest-scoring output from consideration before any sampling
Leaves the probabilities unchanged, as temperature only affects training
quiz.why: Dividing logits by a temperature below 1 widens the gaps between them, so softmax gives the top output a larger share. Temperatures above 1 flatten the distribution instead.

quiz.q: A provider is deciding whether its public API should return log-probabilities for many candidate tokens alongside each generated token. Which risk does this MOST increase?
o: Prompt injection, because attackers can read the system prompt from the values
Model extraction and membership inference, which exploit fine-grained scores
Denial of service, because log-probabilities double the cost of each request
Data poisoning, because users can submit their own scores back into training
quiz.why: Detailed scores reveal how confident the model is and where its decision boundaries lie, which helps attackers copy the model or test whether records were in its training data. Researchers used such API features to recover part of production models in 2024.

quiz.q: A language model’s average cross-entropy per token on a test set falls after further training. What happens to its perplexity on that set?
o: It rises, since perplexity grows as a model becomes more accurate
It decreases too, since perplexity is the exponential of that loss
It stays the same, since perplexity depends only on vocabulary size
It doubles, since perplexity is twice the average loss per token
quiz.why: Perplexity is the exponential of the average cross-entropy per token, so the two move together: lower loss means lower perplexity and better prediction.

exam.q: A bank trains a fraud model with federated learning across its branches, so customer data never leaves each branch. Which risk does this design introduce that centralised training does not?
o: Raw customer data must be copied to a central server
A compromised participant can submit harmful model updates
The model cannot be retrained once deployed
Labels are no longer required for training
exam.why: Federated learning combines updates from many participants. A malicious or compromised participant can send updates that degrade or manipulate the shared model, so the aggregation step needs safeguards.

exam.q: A vendor’s fraud engine combines a learned risk score with hard-coded rules that block transactions above regulatory limits. How is this design BEST described?
o: Purely symbolic, rule-based AI
Purely statistical machine learning
A hybrid of learned and symbolic approaches
An early form of general intelligence
exam.why: A learned model working alongside explicit, human-written rules is a hybrid design, common in regulated settings where some limits must be guaranteed.

exam.q: Why can gradient-free search methods, such as evolutionary algorithms, be used to probe a model deployed behind an API?
o: They need the model’s training data
They only need the model’s outputs to score candidate inputs
They require administrator access to the model’s weights
They work only on models trained with reinforcement learning
exam.why: Evolutionary search optimises against any score, and a model’s responses can serve as that score. That is why query limits, output minimisation and monitoring matter for exposed models.

exam.q: A log-analysis product uses a plain recurrent neural network on very long event sequences. Which limitation should you expect?
o: It can’t process text, only numerical event codes
Information from early in a long sequence tends to fade
It processes every event in parallel, losing their order
It requires labelled images rather than event sequences
exam.why: Plain RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients, so early information is lost over long sequences. LSTMs, GRUs and transformers were developed partly to address this.

exam.q: Several business units run AI workloads on the same pool of cloud GPUs. Which control MOST directly reduces the risk of one workload reading another’s data from accelerator memory?
o: Quantising every model to 4-bit precision, so less data sits in accelerator memory at once
Isolating workloads with dedicated or partitioned GPUs, and clearing memory between jobs
Moving all training jobs to CPUs, which keep each process’s memory strictly separate
Increasing GPU memory capacity so that workloads never have to share the same memory
exam.why: The risk is residual or shared memory between tenants. Isolation and memory clearing address it directly; quantisation and capacity are unrelated to confidentiality.

exam.q: An organisation must serve a large model on hardware with limited memory and can accept a small loss in accuracy. Which technique BEST fits?
o: Quantisation
Dropout
Backpropagation
Data augmentation
exam.why: Quantisation stores weights at lower precision, reducing memory needs at some cost in accuracy. Dropout and augmentation are training techniques; backpropagation computes gradients.

exam.q: Why does a transformer’s design make untrusted text anywhere in its context a security concern?
o: Transformers ignore text beyond the first sentence, so injected text replaces the real instructions
Self-attention lets every token influence every other, with no built-in trusted/untrusted distinction
Transformers execute any code they read in their context, as long as it is written in Python
Untrusted text in the context automatically retrains the model’s weights during inference
exam.why: All tokens in context can shape the output through self-attention. Separating trusted instructions from untrusted data has to be done by controls around the model.

exam.q: An organisation plans to publish the weights of its image-screening model so that partners can run it locally. Which consequence should the risk assessment highlight MOST?
o: The model will stop working if partners use different graphics processors
Anyone can compute input gradients, making strong evasion attacks far easier
Partners will gain the right to reuse the training data for other purposes
The model’s accuracy will fall, because weights degrade when they are copied
exam.why: Open weights give anyone white-box access, so gradient-based attacks such as PGD can craft evasions directly, and the model also becomes a substitute for transfer attacks. Hardware differences, data rights and copying don’t change the model in these ways.

exam.q: A red team reports that one prompt produced a policy violation in 3 of 50 attempts at a temperature of 0.8. The product owner argues that production uses a temperature of 0, so the finding can be closed. What is the BEST response?
o: Close the finding, as a temperature of 0 makes every output safe and fixed
Retest at production settings, with varied prompts, before deciding anything
Close the finding, since 3 failures in 50 is under a typical 10% tolerance
Keep it open only until the provider confirms the result was a glitch
exam.why: A low temperature makes output for one exact prompt more repeatable, not safe: real users vary their prompts, and settings and models change. Retesting under production settings with variations shows whether the risk is real.

exam.q: A SaaS provider batches requests from different customers through a shared mixture-of-experts model with fixed expert capacity. A customer asks whether another tenant could influence its results. What is the BEST response?
o: Reassure the customer, as one request’s output never depends on another’s
Assess the risk, and consider tenant isolation or a different routing design
Confirm there is no risk, since TLS encryption in transit prevents it
Advise the customer to send shorter prompts, so its tokens are routed first
exam.why: Research in 2024 showed that when routing depends on other requests in a batch, for example through fixed expert capacity, one user’s inputs can change another’s outputs. Encryption in transit and prompt length don’t remove that dependency.
